passage:
Dear Manjula Chechi,
You asked why I didn't forward the message about child-kidnappers in white vans to our family group, when you sent it with three warnings.
Honestly, my first feeling was fear. Anu walks to school. My hand went straight to the forward button.
Then I stopped and asked myself a few things. Who wrote it? There was no name, no place, no date. What did it want me to feel? Scared, and angry at strangers. Who gains if a hundred people panic? Not the children.
I called the local police station's helpline number from their official page. The constable said they had no such reports and that this message had come up in other towns too.
So I didn't send it on. It felt oddly brave, just not pressing a button.
Please do call me before sending the next one. I would rather talk than panic together.
With love,
Yogesh

qa.q: Whom did Yogesh call to check the message?
qa.a: Yogesh called the local police station's helpline number from their official page.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Yogesh felt fear for Anu, who walks to school, and Yogesh's hand went straight to the forward button.

qa.q: Which questions helped Yogesh pause before forwarding?
qa.a: Yogesh asked who wrote it, what it was trying to make people feel, and who gains if a hundred people panic, then checked with an official source.

qa.q: How might Manjula Chechi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Manjula Chechi might feel a little embarrassed, but the warm tone and the invitation to call first make the letter feel caring rather than scolding.

grounding: Yogesh refuses to forward a frightening message after asking who wrote it and why it aims to scare, and checks with an official source instead.

passage:
I'm Shalini, Sunaina, and people think fact-checking is only for journalists. For me it looked like a Tuesday at my office.
Someone on my team forwarded a message: "New manager plans to sack everyone over thirty-five. Share before it's deleted." I'm thirty-six. My stomach went cold.
Everybody was forwarding it. I had it copied, ready.
And then I noticed three things. It had no name on it. It wanted me angry and scared at the same time. And "share before it's deleted" is exactly what you say when you don't want people to check.
So I didn't share. I asked HR directly, in writing. They replied the same afternoon: no such plan, and they'd heard the rumour too.
Nobody thanked me, obviously. It isn't the kind of thing people notice. But one colleague said, "You didn't send it? Okay, I'll hold off too."

qa.q: What did HR reply when Shalini asked in writing?
qa.a: HR replied the same afternoon that there was no such plan and that they had heard the rumour too.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling when the message first arrived?
qa.a: Shalini felt a cold fear, because at thirty-six Shalini was one of the people the message said would be sacked.

qa.q: Which signs made Shalini stop before sharing?
qa.a: The message had no name, tried to stir anger and fear at once, and pushed people to share before it was deleted, which discourages checking.

qa.q: How did Shalini's choice affect the colleague who noticed?
qa.a: Seeing Shalini hold back gave that colleague permission to do the same, so one quiet refusal slowed the rumour further.

grounding: Shalini notices a workplace message is built to stir anger and fear, checks with HR instead of forwarding, and quietly slows the rumour.

passage:
I sit across from Rashmi at the bank branch, so I saw the whole thing.
At about eleven, Kamal rushed over with his phone. "Child-lifting gang in our area! Strangers in a white van. Forward to everyone!" The message had a blurry photo, lots of red text, and "SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS".
Rashmi read it slowly. She didn't forward it. She asked, "Which area? Which date? Who sent it first?" Kamal said it came from his cousin's society group.
She scrolled up and down. "It's trying very hard to scare us," she said, more to herself. Then she rang the police station number printed on our notice board. I heard her say "thank you" and hang up.
"No such complaint," she told Kamal. "The same message went round two years ago in another city."
Kamal looked annoyed for a minute. Then he deleted it. I can't say what she felt. Her hands were steady, though. I'm not sure mine would have been.

qa.q: What was in the message Kamal showed?
qa.a: A blurry photo, lots of red text, and 'SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS'.

qa.q: What might Rashmi have been feeling as she read the message, and what cues suggest it?
qa.a: Rashmi seemed calm and cautious rather than frightened: she read slowly, asked questions and kept her hands steady, though the narrator can't be sure.

qa.q: Which steps did Rashmi take before deciding not to forward?
qa.a: Asking which area, which date and who sent it first, noticing it was built to scare, and ringing the police station to check.

qa.q: How did Kamal react when Rashmi said there was no such complaint?
qa.a: Kamal looked annoyed for a minute, perhaps embarrassed at nearly spreading it, and then deleted the message.

grounding: Shows, through a colleague's eyes, a woman pausing on a frightening forward, asking who sent it and checking before refusing to pass it on.

passage:
Day one, a Tuesday: Simran forwarded a message to her office group without a second look: "Salt stock ending, buy 5 packets today!" By evening the corner shop had run out, and the shopkeeper had doubled his price.
Day four: a new one arrived, all capitals: "Tap water poisoned in Sector 12, DO NOT DRINK." Her thumb hovered. Who gains if I'm scared? she asked herself. Is this trying to make me panic? She checked the municipal office's page. Nothing. She called the building caretaker, who said the tanker tests had come back fine that morning. She didn't forward it.
Day eleven: at dinner her brother Kunal held up his phone. "Petrol strike tomorrow, fill up tonight."
"Who sent it first?" Simran asked.
He didn't know. He put the phone down, grumbling. "You've become boring."
Simran smiled. Boring felt fine.

qa.q: What did the message on day one tell people to do?
qa.a: 'Salt stock ending, buy 5 packets today!'

qa.q: What was going on in Simran's mind when her thumb hovered on day four?
qa.a: Simran felt a flicker of panic but stayed cautious, asking who would gain from her fear and whether the message was trying to make her panic.

qa.q: Which checks did Simran use before deciding not to forward?
qa.a: Looking at the municipal office's page and calling the building caretaker about the tanker tests.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Simran's new habit?
qa.a: Kunal grumbles that Simran has become boring, because her question about who sent it first stops his quick sharing.

grounding: Shows a woman learning over days to ask who benefits from a message and whether it aims to scare, and to not forward what is unchecked.

passage:
Jahnavi, you asked why I never forward anything on the office group. Let me tell you about my first job, at a small newspaper in Madurai, when I was twenty-four.
One evening a typed letter came in: the town's cooperative bank was about to collapse, and everyone should take their money out by Friday. My colleague Selvam wanted it on the front page. "People have a right to know!"
It frightened me too. My own mother's savings were in that bank. But I asked: who sent this, and who gains if half the town rushes to the counter tomorrow? There was no name, only a post-box number.
I held it back until morning and phoned the bank's auditor. The accounts were fine. The post box belonged to a man in a court case with the bank.
"Keerthana, you're a coward," Selvam said, every day for a week. Nothing was printed. Nothing happened. That quiet nothing is what I'm proudest of.

qa.q: What did the typed letter tell people to do?
qa.a: Take their money out of the cooperative bank by Friday.

qa.q: How did young Keerthana feel on reading the letter?
qa.a: Young Keerthana felt frightened too, since Keerthana's own mother's savings were in that bank, yet chose to question the letter.

qa.q: What choice inside the story stopped the rumour?
qa.a: Holding the letter back until morning, asking who gained from a rush, and phoning the bank's auditor, who said the accounts were fine.

qa.q: How did Selvam see Keerthana's decision at the time?
qa.a: Selvam thought people had a right to know and called Keerthana a coward for a week, not seeing the harm a false alarm could do.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how asking who benefits and refusing to print an unchecked scare stopped a rumour, a quiet form of courage.

passage: The mehendi was loud, the dhol thumping, and Simran's phone was at four per cent when the forward reached her colony group: a shaky voice note warning that child-lifters in disguise were roaming the area, "share with every parent NOW". Around her, aunties were already forwarding. Reena, her cousin, grabbed her arm. "Send it to your building group! Their kids play outside." Simran's thumb hovered. Her own heart was racing. Then she made herself ask the questions her journalism professor used to drill. Who made this? No name. Where? No place. Why? To make me too scared to think. And who gets hurt if it's wrong? Any poor stranger walking past a frightened crowd. "I'm not sending it," she said. "Not till someone checks." Reena stared. "What if it's true?" "Then the police will know. Call the station from your phone and ask." Reena did. The duty officer said there were no such reports and asked people to stop forwarding.

qa.q: How much battery did Simran's phone have?
qa.a: Four per cent.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when the forward arrived?
qa.a: Simran felt scared, her heart racing, and tempted to forward it like everyone else.

qa.q: Which questions helped Simran decide?
qa.a: Who made it, where it happened, why it wanted her scared, and who gets hurt if it is wrong; with no answers, she held back and had the police asked.

qa.q: What might happen to a stranger if the voice note kept spreading?
qa.a: An innocent stranger could be surrounded and harmed by a frightened crowd, based on nothing.

grounding: Shows a person asking who made a frightening message and whether it aims to scare, and refusing to forward it unchecked amid pressure.
